title: Two functions from a table: product, quotient, tangent line and a limit

stimulus.title: Values of f, g and their derivatives
stimulus.text: The functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable for all real numbers. The table gives values of the functions and their derivatives at selected values of $x$. No calculator is allowed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Let $h(x) = f(x)g(x)$. Find $h'(2)$. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubric.point: Product rule with the table values: $h'(2) = f'(2)g(2) + f(2)g'(2)$. Not earned by $f'(2)g'(2)$, the product of the derivatives.
accept: the two terms in either order, with table values substituted

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Let $k(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$. Find $k'(3)$. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubric.point: Quotient rule with the table values: $k'(3) = \frac{f'(3)g(3) - f(3)g'(3)}{\left( g(3) \right)^2}$. Not earned with the numerator reversed or the denominator not squared.

parts.sample: By the quotient rule, $k'(x) = \frac{f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{\left( g(x) \right)^2}$. So $k'(3) = \frac{(5)(2) - (3)(3)}{(2)^2} = \frac{10 - 9}{4} = \frac{1}{4}$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Let $m(x) = 4f(x) - \ln x$ for $x > 0$. Write an equation for the line tangent to the graph of $m$ at $x = 1$.

rubric.point: Tangent line through $(1, m(1)) = (1, 16)$ with the slope found: $y = 16 - 9(x - 1)$. The height needs $m(1) = 4(4) - \ln 1 = 16$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt:
(i) Find $\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{f(x) - 6}{x - 4}$. Explain your reasoning.
(ii) Explain why there must be a value $c$, with $1 < c < 4$, such that $g(c) = 0$.

rubric.point: (i) The limit is $f'(4) = 1$, because $f(4) = 6$ makes it the definition of the derivative of $f$ at $x = 4$. The bare answer 1, with no link to $f'(4)$, does not earn the point; neither does writing $\frac{0}{0} = 1$.
(ii) Continuity with its reason: $g$ is differentiable, so $g$ is continuous on $[1, 4]$. Not earned by "$g$ is continuous" with no reason.
accept: g is differentiable, therefore continuous on the interval

rubric.point: (ii) Conclusion, with the continuity point: $g(1) = 1 > 0 > -1 = g(4)$, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a $c$ in $(1, 4)$ with $g(c) = 0$

parts.sample:
(i) Since $f(4) = 6$, $\frac{f(x) - 6}{x - 4} = \frac{f(x) - f(4)}{x - 4}$, so the limit is the definition of $f'(4)$. From the table, $\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{f(x) - 6}{x - 4} = f'(4) = 1$.
(ii) $g$ is differentiable, so $g$ is continuous on $[1, 4]$. Also $g(1) = 1$ and $g(4) = -1$, so 0 is between $g(4)$ and $g(1)$. By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is a value $c$ with $1 < c < 4$ such that $g(c) = 0$.
